title: Aloo Parathas, Saag and Ghee: The Haryanvi Diet That Fuelled Saina Nehwal
excerpt: The badminton legend swears by aloo parathas, sarson ka saag and ghee — and dietitians explain why the Haryanvi thali works, and how to eat it without her training load.
body:
• Saina Nehwal revealed her daily diet in a chat with macrobiotic coach Dr Shilpa Arora: aloo parathas, milk with almond or badam oil, rajma, kadhi and chole with rice — the Haryanvi food she grew up on.
  • Her two favourite dishes are aloo paratha and saag; she insists ghee is essential — "joints ke liye bohot zaruri hai" (crucial for the joints).
  • Dietitians say the meals balance protein, carbohydrates and healthy fats — but warn the calorie load works only because she burns it off in rigorous training.
  • If you eat this way without an athlete's training load: pair parathas with curd or vegetables to slow digestion, keep portions in check, and don't load ghee beyond a spoon or two a day.

Badminton legend Saina Nehwal was born in Hisar, Haryana, and moved to Hyderabad only when her training began in earnest. The secret to her energy, she says, lies in desi, ghee-laden meals from her mother's kitchen. In a candid chat with macrobiotic coach Dr Shilpa Arora on her YouTube channel, Nehwal laid out what she eats on a normal day: a lot of "Haryana-style" food — aloo parathas, milk with a dash of almond or badam oil, rajma, kadhi and chole paired with rice.

Aloo paratha and saag are two of her all-time favourite dishes. And she is emphatic about ghee: "Joints ke liye bohot zaruri hai (It's crucial for the joints)," she said. Her mother added, "Ever since she was a young girl, I fed her ghee and oil to give her strength."

There is, however, a catch that Nehwal herself flags: she doesn't let the fat accumulate. She burns it off through rigorous training — the kind of daily load that bears no resemblance to a desk job.

"Joints ke liye bohot zaruri hai (It's crucial for the joints)."

— Saina Nehwal, on ghee

Decoding the diet

Deepalakshmi, a registered dietitian at Shree Balaji Medical Centre in Chennai, says Nehwal's meals are an excellent balance of protein and carbohydrates, with a side of healthy fats. "Ghee is rich in healthy fats, which help the digestive system, strengthen the immune system, and are rich in vitamins," she told the Indian Express. Ghee also contains butyrate, a compound that strengthens intestinal cells and supports smoother digestion.

Sarson ka saag — slow-cooked mustard greens, often with spinach or bathua, flavoured with ginger, garlic and ghee — brings dietary fibre and prebiotics. "Mustard greens are rich in dietary fibre and prebiotics and are gentle on the stomach," Deepalakshmi said, adding that the plant compounds in mustard leaves help reduce gut inflammation. A little ghee, she notes, helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K from the greens — the body cannot use these fat-soluble nutrients without dietary fat.

Edwina Raj, Head of Services for Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics at Aster CMI Hospital in Bangalore, adds the other half of the picture: aloo parathas give quick energy because they are high in carbohydrates, which may raise blood sugar — and because they are often made with oil, butter or ghee, they are calorie-dense. "Eating it with curd or vegetables slows digestion and reduces the blood sugar spike because they add protein and fibre," she said, recommending pairing parathas with protein, fibre or low-fat sides to keep energy steady and blood sugar under control.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, this is less a diet plan than a vindication — the foods many of us were told to give up in favour of "clean eating" are what fuelled a world No. 1 and an Olympic medallist. The practical takeaway from the dietitians is simple and cheap: keep the ghee but measure it, pair heavy carb plates with curd or vegetables, and if you have weak digestion or IBS, tread carefully — Deepalakshmi warns such heavy meals can be hard to digest, and suggests curd or buttermilk for its probiotics.

What's next

Nehwal's generation of athletes trained through an era when sports nutrition in India meant mother's kitchen plus discipline. The science now catches up: the combination of complex carbs, fermented dairy and fat-soluble vitamins in the Haryanvi thali was doing more than anyone credited it with. The lesson isn't to eat like an Olympian — it's that the humble thali, eaten sensibly, was never the problem.
